title: Acupuncture Exposed: What the Evidence Really Says
description:
Acupuncture is often praised as an ancient Chinese medicine that balances energy, cures pain, and has “no side effects.” But what does the evidence really say? In this episode of Pale Blue Thoughts, we expose the myths of acupuncture and reveal why it’s more placebo than proven treatment.

We trace its origins from sharp stones in 6000 BCE, to meridian theories in old Chinese texts, to the revival of acupuncture during Mao’s barefoot doctor campaign. Even Otzi the Iceman’s tattoos suggest acupuncture-like ideas existed outside China. Yet, despite the mystical claims of qi, meridians, and acupoints, science has never found them.

Modern studies show acupuncture only seems to help with pain and post-surgery nausea, and even then, sham needles, toothpicks, or just touching the skin work just as well. In reality, acupuncture’s effects are explained by the placebo effect, false positives in poorly designed studies, and patient belief. Claims that it cures everything from AIDS to addiction collapse under scrutiny.

We also uncover the risks: infections, collapsed lungs, and even deaths linked to acupuncture needles. Variants like ear acupuncture, micro acupuncture, moxibustion, and homeopathic injections only add to the pseudoscience circus. After thousands of clinical trials, the verdict is clear: acupuncture is not evidence-based medicine.

👉 If you’ve searched for acupuncture, acupuncture myths, acupuncture debunked, acupuncture placebo effect, acupuncture risks, does acupuncture work, qi, meridians, acupoints, acupuncture pseudoscience — this video gives you the rational perspective.

Now, there was a study called the Cactus study. It compared regular care to regular care plus acupuncture. The problem was it was a badly designed study and it didn't include any fake acupuncture controls. The study concluded that adding 12 sessions of five element acupuncture to regular care improved health and well-being for a year. But here's the catch. When you add something to regular care, you're likely to see some improvement even if it's not because of the added treatment. So, a study without proper controls doesn't really tell us much. The most well-designed acupuncture studies with solid sham controls have taught us some important lessons. It turns out that the exact placement of the needles doesn't really matter. It also doesn't matter whether you use real needles or pretended ones. In one study, just gently touching the skin with a toothpick had the same effect. What does matter is whether the patients believe they are receiving real acupuncture. If they got acupuncture, but believed it was fake, it didn't work. On the flip side, if they didn't get acupuncture, but thought they did, it worked just as well as the real thing. People always think acupuncture is completely safe, but that is not always true. Doctors shouldn't lie to patients, and if patients think they are better when they are not, it can cause trust issues, and it may not be good for their health. So, while placebos can sometimes help, they have their problems in medicine. While placebos can help some patients in the short run, remember they are not an actual cure. Think about a patient who may have a life-threatening disease. If they put their faith on a placebo-based medicine, they would be forgoing a proper treatment that could have cured them or extended their life to the very least. In simple terms, acupuncture seems to help with some types of pain and feeling queasy after surgery. But for everything else, like treating specific medical conditions, it doesn't seem to do much. The ideas behind acupuncture doesn't really make sense from a medical standpoint. All you will get from people who have attended such treatments are anecdotal evidences similar to homeopathy and Ayurveda. I have said this multiple times now and I repeat, anecdotal evidences are just data, not conclusive and deserves the dustbin. Some people argue that we need more studies on acupuncture, but after thousands of trials, it's fair to question whether it is worth the time and money.
